passage: I'm Jyoti, Ankita's cousin, and we walk to school together, so I've seen this whole thing. It's been nine days since Ankita stopped talking to Megha. At first Megha kept coming up to her: in the corridor, at the gate, with notes, once with Ankita's favourite chikki. Ankita would look away, but I saw the tiny smile when Megha walked off. She liked being chased, I think. Now Megha has stopped trying as much, and Ankita keeps checking the gate anyway. Yesterday she ate lunch alone and said she preferred it. Last night she told me, "If I talk now, after nine days, it'll look so stupid." Then she stared at her phone till the screen went dark.

qa.q: What did Megha once bring Ankita?
qa.a: Megha once brought Ankita's favourite chikki.

qa.q: What does Ankita's tiny smile when Megha walked off suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she enjoyed being chased and wanted back, even while keeping up the silence.

qa.q: What turning point is still open to Ankita after nine days?
qa.a: She could send Megha a simple message, "I've been silly and I miss you, can we talk?", accepting a moment of embarrassment instead of weeks more.

qa.q: What might Megha be going through now that Megha has stopped trying so much?
qa.a: Megha may feel tired and rejected after days of notes and chikki with no reply, and may now be guarding against more hurt.

grounding: Shows, through a cousin's eyes, a teen whose silence has become a punishment she half enjoys, while loneliness and embarrassment grow each day.

passage:
Day 2: Jomon walked past Avni's desk without a word. She'd laughed at his poem in Malayalam class, and he wanted her to work that out on her own. When she whispered, "Jomon, what's wrong?", he felt a small, warm thrill. She cared.
Day 6: Avni had asked four more times. He still said nothing. At home he opened their chat, typed "you know what you did", and deleted it. The house felt very quiet. He missed her voice notes about cricket.
Day 11: Avni had stopped asking. Jomon sat alone at recess, rehearsing ways to break the silence. Every version sounded more ridiculous than the last. After eleven days, how do you just say hi?

qa.q: What did Jomon type and delete on Day 6?
qa.a: He typed "you know what you did" and deleted it.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel when Avni whispered "Jomon, what's wrong?" on Day 2?
qa.a: He felt a small, warm thrill, taking it as proof that she cared.

qa.q: What small step could Jomon take on Day 11?
qa.a: He could tell Avni directly, "The laugh at my poem hurt, and I stayed silent too long. Sorry", since a short honest line beats a perfect speech.

qa.q: How might Avni be feeling by Day 11?
qa.a: Avni has probably stopped asking out of hurt or confusion, not knowing that the laugh at the poem started it.

grounding: Shows a teen whose silence turns into a message of 'you should know', enjoying being wanted yet growing lonelier as speaking gets harder.

passage:
Harish, come sit by your grandmother. You're not talking to your friend? I'll tell you something about me, Lalremsiami, when I was fifteen in Aizawl.
My friend forgot my birthday. I didn't say a word. I just stopped talking to her.
Day one, I felt powerful. She kept coming to my desk, asking, and I liked that she wanted me back.
Day four, I was lonely. I ate lunch alone and pretended to read.
Day seven, I wanted to talk to her so badly. But how could I? After a whole week of silence, just saying "hi" felt ridiculous. My silence was saying: you ought to work out your own mistake. But she didn't.
It took me a month. A whole month, for a birthday.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami's friend forget?
qa.a: Her birthday.

qa.q: What was young Lalremsiami feeling by day seven?
qa.a: She felt lonely and wanted to talk, but embarrassed, because after a week of silence even saying "hi" felt ridiculous.

qa.q: In the story, when was the easiest moment for young Lalremsiami to break the silence?
qa.a: On day one, when her friend kept coming to her desk to ask, she could have told her about the birthday; each day after made it harder.

qa.q: What was the friend likely experiencing during the silence?
qa.a: She probably felt confused and anxious, not knowing what she had done, since she kept asking.

grounding: A grandmother recalls how, as a teen, her silence became a punishment; she enjoyed being wanted back yet grew lonelier, and breaking it felt more embarrassing each day.

passage:
Dolma and Hansa had to finish the science model together by Friday, and they hadn't spoken since Monday.
It had started when Hansa told the others about Dolma's crush. Dolma had gone silent. Now it was Thursday, the model was half-glued, and they passed the glue stick without a word.
Hansa kept trying. "Should the volcano be red or orange?" "Dolma, please." Dolma liked that Hansa kept trying. It felt like proof.
But at night, Dolma felt awful. Lonelier than ever. She wanted to say something, anything. But after four days, what would she even say? It would look like she'd lost.
She painted the volcano orange, and said nothing.

qa.q: When did the science model have to be finished?
qa.a: By Friday.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling at night?
qa.a: She felt awful and lonelier than ever, wanting to speak but embarrassed that breaking the silence after four days would look like losing.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Dolma while they work on the model?
qa.a: She could answer Hansa's question about the colour and add one honest sentence about why she was hurt, rather than letting the silence harden further.

qa.q: What might Hansa be experiencing as she keeps trying?
qa.a: She is probably guilty and anxious, trying to reach Dolma and not getting any answer.

grounding: A teenage girl's silence hardens into punishment; she enjoys being wanted back but feels lonelier, and breaking it grows more embarrassing each day.

passage:
On the fifth day, Neelam stopped trying. She walked past Hrithik's building without looking up at his window.
Hrithik watched from his balcony in the colony and felt a strange jolt. For four days he'd enjoyed it: her messages, her waiting at the gate, her "please just tell me." He hadn't answered one. She should know what she did. She'd told everyone his marks.
But now she'd stopped. And the room felt very quiet.
He picked up his phone. Put it down. What would he even type, after five days? "Hi"? It would look ridiculous. It would look like he'd given in.
He stayed on the balcony till the streetlights came on.

qa.q: What had Neelam told everyone, according to Hrithik?
qa.a: His marks.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling when Neelam stopped trying?
qa.a: He felt a jolt of loneliness and emptiness, and embarrassment at the idea of breaking the silence after five days.

qa.q: What turning point is still open to Hrithik?
qa.a: He could send one short message, even an awkward one, telling Neelam what hurt, instead of waiting for her to guess.

qa.q: What might Neelam be experiencing on the fifth day?
qa.a: She likely feels hurt and tired of trying, giving up after four days of messages with no answer.

grounding: A teenage boy's silence becomes a punishment; he enjoyed being wanted back, but when his friend stops trying he feels lonelier and embarrassed to break it.

passage:
"Tenzing called again," said Pallavi didi, holding out Irfan's phone. "Fourth time today."

"Let it ring."

"What did he even do?"

"He knows what he did."

"Does he? Because he told Ammi he has no idea."

Irfan shrugged, but he didn't let go of the phone. "He left me out of the cricket team photo. On purpose."

"Did you tell him that?"

"I shouldn't have to."

Pallavi sat on his bed. "It's been six days, Irfan."

"Yeah." He stared at the screen. It felt good, a bit, that Tenzing kept trying. But he'd eaten lunch alone all week, and last night he'd almost called, then felt stupid. "If I call now, after six days, it'll look like I was wrong. It's too weird."

"It'll be weirder at twelve days," she said.

qa.q: How many days had Irfan not spoken to Tenzing?
qa.a: It had been six days.

qa.q: What is Irfan feeling about breaking the silence now?
qa.a: He feels embarrassed and lonely; he likes being wanted back but thinks calling after six days would look like admitting he was wrong.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Irfan now?
qa.a: He could call Tenzing and just say what hurt, the photo, since the longer he waits the harder it will be.

qa.q: How might Tenzing be experiencing these six days?
qa.a: Tenzing seems confused and worried, calling repeatedly and telling Ammi he has no idea what he did.

grounding: A teen's silence hardens into a message, 'you should know', and though he enjoys being wanted back he grows lonelier and more embarrassed each day.
